parole.testo: From amaro (“bitter”) + -one (augmentative suffix), a likely calque of Venetan amaron.
Borrowed from Venetan ancoi, derived from an unknown term + Latin hodiē (“today”). Compare Ligurian ancheu.
From Venetan [Term?], itself from Ancient Greek ἅρπαξ (hárpax, “grappling-iron; flesh-hook”).

parole.significato: either of the three judges, in the old Venetian republic, who were in charge of judicial and constitutional matters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan avogadore, from Latin advocātōrem.

parole.significato: a type of biscuit from Venice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan baìcoło.

parole.significato: title and function borne by an envoy of the Most Serene Republic of Venice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan bailo, ultimately from Latin baiulus. Doublet of balivo and balì.

parole.significato: the stick of a zanni in the commedia dell'arte, most notably of Harlequin and Brighella; behind the scenes it works as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan batocio, due to it being used by Harlequin, a Venetian mask. Doublet of batacchio, batocchio, and battaglio.
From archaic or regional bigolone, from Venetan bigoli (“spaghetti; (dialectal slang) euphemism for body part”).
Borrowed from Venetan bocia, probably from Italian boccia, either in the sense of “wooden ball (for the game of bocce)” or in the jocular sense of “young boy”, sometimes as well of "head".
From Venetan.
Borrowed from Venetan branza, from branchia (“gill”).
Borrowed from Venetan, from Latin calamus. Doublet of calamo.
Borrowed from Venetan camaroto.

parole.significato: credit establishment, originally founded by Tuscan bankers in Piedmont, Italy
parole.testo: From Venetan casnà (“treasure; heap of money”), itself from Arabic خزينة (ḵazīna, “treasure”), via Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (hazna), from whence Turkish hazine (“treasure”). Influenced by casa (“house”).

parole.significato: a type of peasant's house in the Veneto
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan caxon.
From earlier catastro, a borrowing from Venetan catastico, from Byzantine Greek κατάστιχον (katástikhon, “line by line”).

parole.significato: a covered shelter for boats (typical of Venice and the Veneto)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan cavana, from Late Latin cabanna, capanna. Doublet of capanna.

Ultimately from German Kutsche, likely via Venetan cocio, which would explain why /t͡ʃ/ was adapted as /kkj/ (compare Venetan ocio : Italian occhio).
From Venetan.

parole.significato: dukedom, duchy (of a Venetian doge), dogate
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Venetan dogado, from Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of Latin dux (“duke; leader”) + -ātus. Compare ducato and dogato.

parole.significato: dogaressa, dogess (the wife of a doge)
parole.testo: Venetan dogaresa, from Medieval Latin ducarissa, from Latin ducatrix, from dux (“ruler”) + -issa (feminine suffix), with an additional infix. By surface analysis, doge + -essa. Doublet of duchessa.

parole.significato: dukedom, duchy (of a Venetian doge), dogate
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing from Venetan dogado, from Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of Latin dux (“duke; leader”) + -ātus. By surface analysis, doge + -ato. Doublet of ducato and dogado.
Borrowed from Venetan doxe, from Latin ducem (“leader; commander; ruler”). Doublet of duce and duca.

parole.significato: the peculiar smell left on dishes, glasses and kitchenware after having been used for fish, egg or milk products; also…
parole.testo: From Venetan freschin.

Disputed. First attested in 1914, originally as a dialectal Roman word. Compare earlier Neapolitan froscio (“flabby, flaccid; idiot, stupid person”), akin to floscio, and Sicilian frociu (“idiot, coward”). Compare also Venetan fenocio (“gay man”) and Emilian fnòč (“gay man”), akin to synonymous fino

Borrowed in the 17th century from Venetan gazeta (“newspaper”), from gazeta dele novità (literally “a gazeta (halfpenny) of news”), named for the cost (one gazeta) of the newspaper. Borrowed from Venetan ghèto (“foundry”). Alternatively a clipping of borghetto, diminutive of borgo (“village”). Initially used of the areas Jews were concentrated, later extended to concentrations of other ethnicities and then non-ethnic groups.
From Venetan gnoco, perhaps from Lombard knohhil (“knot in wood”). Doublet of nocchio.
Borrowed from Venetan góndoła, probably from Byzantine Greek κοντοῦρα (kontoûra, “small tail”).
Borrowed from Venetan, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *cancricula, diminutive of Classical Latin cancer (“crab”).
Borrowed from Venetan graspo.
From Venetan imbrenà (literally “bridled”).
Borrowed from Venetan lovo (“wolf”), from Latin lupus. Doublet of lupo and lupus.

parole.significato: a thin pork sausage from the Veneto
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan luganega.

parole.significato: a light punt used for fishing, racing and recreation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan, related to mascheretta.

parole.significato: blotched picarel (Spicara maena, a fish of the Mediterranean and Atlantic)
parole.testo: From a Venetan dialect term derived from a diminutive of Latin maena.

parole.significato: a spirit made by distilling vino cotto
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan.

parole.significato: sluggish, listless, depressed, downcast, disheartened, crestfallen, dejected
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Venetan mogio (“soaked, damp”), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“to soak”), from Latin mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: a shore crab (Carcinus maenas) fished and sold as food right after the shedding of the shell
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan moleca.

parole.significato: a small fishing net on the end of a long, wooden handle
parole.testo: From Venetan [Term?].

parole.significato: a type of Venetian street sign painted directly on the plaster of walls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan niçiołeto, nisiołeto, a diminutive of niçioło, nisioło (“cloth; bedsheet”), from Latin linteolum (“linen cloth”). By surface analysis, lenzuolo + -etto.

parole.significato: name of several kinds of water plants, such as sedges, reedmaces, rushes etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan pavera~paviera.
From Venetan petegolar, from petegolo (“gossip”, noun), from peto (“fart”).
From Venetan pòrtego. Doublet of portico.

parole.significato: a member of the senate of the Republic of Venice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan. Compare Italian pregato.

parole.significato: unwanted air bubble which forms inside glass
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan pùłega (literally “flea”), used by Venetian glassmakers such as those from Murano. The term is from Vulgar Latin *pūlica (“flea”), from Latin pūlex, from Proto-Indo-European *plus-. Doublet of pulce.
From Venetan form of quarantina.
Borrowed from Venetan regatar, possibly from Vulgar Latin *recaptāre.

parole.significato: a traditional Venetian dish, similar to a risotto, made from new peas and rice and flavored with pancetta
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan rixi e bixi (“rice[s] and peas”).
Borrowed from Venetan. Compare Italian rogato.
Borrowed from Venetan sardeła. Doublet of sardella.

parole.significato: small lobster, typically Nephrops norvegicus, aka langoustine or Dublin Bay prawn. Sometimes incorrectly used more gene…
parole.testo: From Venetan scampo, from Ancient Greek κάμπος (kámpos, “sea monster”), or Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ, “bending, bow”).
Borrowed from Venetan.
Verb-object compound, composed of scopa (“to sweep”) + mare (“sea”); Calque of Venetan scoamàr.

parole.significato: swab, pull through (for cleaning a gun), pipe cleaner
parole.testo: A diminutive based on Venetan scova, the counterpart to Italian scopa (“broom”). Compare Sicilian scupinu.

parole.significato: an alley that passes underneath a building
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan sotopòrtego, cognate to sottoportico, from soto- (“under-”) + pòrtego (“porch”).

parole.significato: a character type representing a servant who is either an astute trickster or a silly jester
parole.testo: From Zanni, from Venetan Zani, alteration of the given name Gianni, itself a hypocorism for Giovanni.
